strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for vision-language data collection: whether captions naturally authored in different languages provide complementary visual information. This empirical contribution has potential value independently of benchmark-leading performance.

The comparison framework holds images and caption-set sizes fixed and includes monolingual baselines across languages. Consistent coverage increases across human captions, LLaVA, and Vertex provide useful evidence of language-associated differences.

The Visual Genome experiment strengthens the semantic findings by checking annotated objects. Table 3 reports coverage increasing from 9.6% to 11.5% for Vertex and from 9.5% to 12.0% for LLaVA when comparing English-only sets with the multilingual average.

The translation evaluation and additional human study provide valuable validation efforts. The study involving 20 English/Japanese speakers and 30 images reports complementary coverage gains of 8.4% for objects, 7.7% for relations, and 6.5% for attributes.
weaknesses: Quantitative inconsistencies undermine confidence in important results. Every entry in the 6×6 LLaVA fine-tuning table (Table 14) exactly matches the corresponding subset of the Vertex table (Table 4), despite supposedly different training and evaluation captions. Table 2 reports a Vertex monolingual attribute average of 1.98, although its entries average approximately 1.69. Section 2.2 also attributes aggregate percentage gains to a specific English/French/Chinese comparison that yields different gains. These discrepancies affect replication and effect-size claims, beyond cosmetic presentation.

The expressive measurements are insufficiently validated. LIWC tone, authenticity, and related scores are computed after GPT-4 translation, but the human evaluation assesses semantic preservation rather than preservation of these expressive properties. Appendix 8.1 also samples model-generated captions rather than the human XM captions. Near-chance source-language prediction by one linear classifier cannot establish that translation artifacts are absent, and untranslated multilingual embeddings retain language identity.

Larger scene-graph unions establish broader extracted coverage, but their interpretation as richer accurate visual information needs stronger measurement controls. The paper provides no quantitative parser-error audit, sensitivity analysis for concept merging, or caption-length control. Visual Genome object recall partially addresses grounding, but does not validate additional relations and attributes or measure whether greater coverage accompanies more hallucinated content.

The inference in Section 3.2 is technically unsupported. Similar diversity between multilingual outputs from one model and English outputs from several models does not rule out language-specific internal modes; the assumed ordering between these sources of variation is unjustified. Likewise, shared annotation instructions do not separate language effects from annotator population and cultural differences. The evidence supports distributional association more strongly than the proposed explanations.

Fine-tuning primarily demonstrates adaptation to reference-caption distributions. It does not establish improved visual representations. Moreover, Table 10 identifies multilingual training as best on multilingual evaluation, while French-only training scores higher in Table 4 (0.246 versus 0.244) and Table 15 (0.154 versus 0.151). Table 15 also contradicts the universal matching-language claim for Chinese. These exceptions should constrain the conclusions drawn from this experiment.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are inadequate: exact model checkpoints, decoding settings, fine-tuning hyperparameters, split seeds, and concept-merging thresholds are missing. The primary coverage and fine-tuning tables lack confidence intervals or sufficiently specified significance tests. The useful descriptive findings merit consideration, but the combination of unresolved quantitative inconsistencies and insufficient validation of central measurements currently favors weak rejection.
